Stage 3 · Reading

The box that arrived in Philadelphia

Twenty-seven hours, three states, and four men waiting in an office for a crate marked “dry goods”.

📦🔒
1 · Before you read. The crate was labelled “dry goods” and “this side up”. What does the second label tell you?

Choose one and say why. Compare with a partner before you read.Choose one and say why before you read.Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against the text.

The box that arrived in Philadelphia

Written for this course, from Encyclopedia Virginia, the Pennsylvania Center for the Book, and the Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on Henry ‘Box’ Brown.

1By six o’clock on the morning of 24 March 1849, four men in a Philadelphia office had already been waiting for two hours. They had been told to expect a wooden crate from Richmond, in Virginia, labelled as dry goods. They had not been told what to do if it arrived closed and silent. All four were tense. When the wagon finally came in from a muddy yard, the driver, who had been given no explanation at all, looked puzzled at how many people had gathered for one box.

2Inside was Henry Brown, who had been born into slavery in Louisa County, Virginia, around 1815, and who had been sent at fifteen to work in a tobacco factory in Richmond. He had been treated less harshly than many; he had married, and he had been paying his wife’s owner, out of his own wages, not to sell her. In 1848 she and their three children were sold to a buyer in another state anyway. Brown was furious, and then, for months, simply miserable. Every promise he had relied on had turned out to be worth nothing, and the bitter clarity that followed decided everything he did next.

3The plan was his own. Through James C. A. Smith, a free Black man who sang in the same church choir, he reached Samuel A. Smith, a white shoemaker who agreed to help for a fee. Brown had saved 166 dollars and handed over 86 of them. A carpenter had built the crate to order: roughly three feet long, two and a half deep, two wide, with holes bored for air. It was consigned to the Adams Express Company, which had built a reputation for asking no questions, and addressed to James Miller McKim of the Pennsylvania Anti-Slavery Society. Letters had been exchanged for weeks beforehand to ensure that somebody would be in the office when it came.

4The journey took twenty-seven hours and used almost every kind of transport then available: wagon, railway, steamboat, ferry, and wagon again. For several of those hours the box had been left upside down, and Brown, who could not move and could not call out, later wrote that he had felt the blood forcing itself into his head and had been certain he was dying. He had been given a little water and a few biscuits, and nothing else. Petrified of making a sound, he had lain still through all of it. At least twice, anxious handlers who were puzzled by the weight had come close to opening it.

5When the lid came off he was disorientated and could not stand. The men, who had been terrified that they had waited too long, were enormously relieved, and then delighted. Within weeks Brown had become a speaker on the anti-slavery circuit; at a convention in New England he was introduced by the nickname that stayed with him, and by September a narrative of the escape had been published. Not everybody approved. Frederick Douglass was upset that the method had been described in print at all, since printing it had closed the route for anybody who might have used it afterwards.

6The warning was justified. When Samuel Smith tried to send others north the same way later that year, he was arrested and sentenced to years in the Virginia penitentiary. Brown himself left for England after the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, toured for years with a huge moving panorama of scenes from slavery, and ended his working life on stage as a magician. Historians have since investigated the route, the dates and the paperwork in detail. But his legacy is not really the box. It is what he did with the story once he was out of it.

Text A · Twenty-seven hours

Written for this course, from Encyclopedia Virginia and the Pennsylvania Center for the Book.

They had been told to expect a wooden crate from Richmond, in Virginia, labelled as dry goods. They had not been told what to do if it arrived closed and silent. All four were tense. When the wagon finally came in from a muddy yard, the driver, who had been given no explanation at all, looked puzzled at how many people had gathered for one box.

Inside was Henry Brown, who had been born into slavery in Louisa County, Virginia, around 1815, and who had been sent at fifteen to a tobacco factory in Richmond. He had been treated less harshly than many; he had married, and he had been paying his wife’s owner, out of his own wages, not to sell her. In 1848 she and their three children were sold to a buyer in another state anyway. Brown was furious, and then, for months, simply miserable. The journey took twenty-seven hours, using almost every kind of transport then available: wagon, railway, steamboat, ferry, wagon again. For several of those hours the box had been left upside down, and Brown, who could not move and could not call out, later wrote that he had felt the blood forcing itself into his head and had been certain he was dying. Text B · What the story cost

Written for this course, from the Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on Henry ‘Box’ Brown and the Pennsylvania Center for the Book.

The plan had been Brown’s own. Through James C. A. Smith, a free Black man who sang in the same church choir, he had reached Samuel A. Smith, a white shoemaker who agreed to help for a fee. Brown had saved 166 dollars and handed over 86 of them. A carpenter had built the crate to order: roughly three feet long, two and a half deep, two wide, with holes bored for air. It was consigned to the Adams Express Company, which had built a reputation for asking no questions, and addressed to James Miller McKim of the Pennsylvania Anti-Slavery Society. Letters had been exchanged for weeks beforehand to ensure that somebody would be in the office when it came.

Within weeks of his arrival Brown had become a speaker on the anti-slavery circuit; at a convention in New England he was introduced by the nickname that stayed with him, and by September a narrative of the escape had been published. Not everybody approved. Frederick Douglass was upset that the method had been described in print at all, since printing it had closed the route for anybody who might have used it afterwards.

The warning was justified. When Samuel Smith tried to send others north the same way later that year, he was arrested and sentenced to years in the Virginia penitentiary. Brown himself left for England after the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, toured for years with a huge moving panorama of scenes from slavery, and ended his working life on stage as a magician. Historians have since investigated the route, the dates and the paperwork in detail. But his legacy is not really the box. It is what he did with the story once he was out of it.

5 · One solved transformation, step by step.
Worked example

Start. Somebody promised Brown that his family would not be sold. Then they were sold.

Step 1 — put the earlier event in the past perfect. The promise came first, so: Somebody had promised Brown that his family would not be sold.

Step 2 — make it passive, because the promiser does not matter. Move Brown to the front, keep had, add been, keep the participle: Brown had been promised that his family would not be sold.

Check. Two things must still be true: the promise is clearly earlier than the sale, and Brown is the subject of his own sentence. Both are.

1 · Read the explanation.
One auxiliary, three forms

Every past perfect begins with had, and had never changes for person: I had, she had, they had. What follows decides which of the three forms you are using.

Simple: had + past participle. A carpenter had built the crate. Continuous: had been + -ing. They had been waiting for two hours. Passive: had been + past participle. He had been promised otherwise.

Notice that the continuous and the passive both contain had been. Only the word after it tells you which is which: -ing means continuous, a participle means passive.

Choosing between them
  • Simple or continuous? The simple form packages the event: they had waited two hours. The continuous leaves it running and stresses the length: they had been waiting two hours. With state verbs (know, be, believe) only the simple form is possible.
  • Active or passive? Use the passive when the doer is unknown, unimportant, or deliberately left out — and to keep the person the story is about as the subject of the sentence.
  • Negatives carry weight. In this story, they had not been told and he had never suffered do as much work as anything positive. The past perfect is often used to say what had not happened yet.

Two things to watch

1 — Had been waiting and had been told look identical and are not. One is continuous, one is passive. Read the word after been: waiting is -ing, told is a participle.

2 — Do not use the past perfect for the main story. Once you have stepped back and explained the background, come forward again into the past simple. A paragraph written entirely in the past perfect has no story left in it.

12 · Read this before the extra practice.
One form, four shapes

The past perfect is had plus a past participle, and had never changes for person: A carpenter had built the crate · They had built it together. The negative puts not after had (He had not suffered that before) and the question puts the subject after it (Had anybody opened it?). In speech had reduces to ’d, which is why learners often lose it altogether in writing.

The continuous is had been + -ing and gives the length or the ongoing quality of something before the story reached that point: They had been waiting for two hours. The passive is had been + past participle and is used when who did it is unknown or beside the point: He had been promised otherwise · They had not been told what was inside. Note that the two share the words had been: what follows decides which one you are reading.

What the negative does in a story

In a narrative the past perfect negative often carries more weight than the positive, because it names the thing that was missing and explains everything that follows: Nobody had checked the crate, They had not been told where it was going, He had never travelled by air before. Each of these is a cause dressed as a fact.

Time markers that pull the past perfect towards them: by the time, by then, already, just, never … before, until then, it was the first time. Note the last one: It was the first time he had flown — the clause after the first time takes the past perfect when the reference point is in the past.

Errors to watch: He had went → had gone · They had been told nothing by nobody → had been told nothing · He had been promised by the company otherwise is possible but heavy — leave the agent out unless it matters · It was the first time he flew → had flown.

1 · Read the model.
Model · a letter written the same evening

My dear James,

It is nearly midnight and I am still not steady, so forgive the hand.

The letter had reached us eleven days ago and we had expected the crate on the 23rd. When nothing came, two of us went home convinced that it had been opened somewhere on the road. I had not slept since. This morning we were all four in the office by six, and by eight we had been standing at that window for two hours without speaking.

The wagon came in through the yard at a walking pace. The driver had been told nothing and looked at us as though we were mad. We carried it in, and I remember being certain, for perhaps ten seconds, that we had come too late.

Then the lid came off. He could not stand, and he was disorientated for some minutes, but he spoke, and I have never in my life been so relieved. What I shall remember is not the box. It is that we had all been so tense we had forgotten to open the window, and the first thing he asked for was air.
